We got offered a 45-minute afternoon slot at a major festival. The fee is lower than our hard ticket club guarantee. Should we take it? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

When evaluating a festival offer with a lower fee than your hard ticket guarantee, the first thing you must check is the radius clause. Major festivals typically enforce a 60-to-90 day, 100-mile radius clause. This means if you accept the festival, you are legally barred from booking your own headline club show in that market for months. You have to calculate if the festival exposure is worth cannibalizing your own higher-paying hard ticket play.

Secondly, consider the production reality. Afternoon festival slots rarely include soundchecks; you will get a 15-minute changeover and a line check. If your set relies heavily on complex track routing and automated lighting, it may not translate well in a fast-and-dirty daylight setting. 

However, the strategic value can be massive. Playing a major festival puts you in front of a completely new audience, provides excellent leverage for your booking agent to secure better support tours, and offers high-value networking in VIP areas. If your tour budget can absorb the lower fee, and you plan to return to that market for a headline play 6 months later to capture the new fans, taking the festival slot is usually the right long-term career move.

I've been booking my own shows and it's exhausting. When should I get a booking agent and how do I find one? [Context: {"currentModule":"road","hasProject":true}]

Booking agents are the gatekeepers to better venues, higher guarantees, and efficient routing. But timing matters — approach too early and you'll get ignored. Here's the full playbook:

When you're ready for an agent: (1) You can consistently draw 50-100+ people in your home market. (2) You've done at least one self-booked tour (proving you can sell tickets outside your city). (3) You have a growing online presence (10k+ followers helps, but draw is more important). (4) You're earning $300-$1,000+ per show in guarantees. (5) Venues are responding to YOUR emails (not ghosting you).

What a booking agent does: Negotiates guarantees and deal structures with venues/promoters. Routes tours efficiently (minimizing long drives between shows). Opens doors to venues and festivals you can't access yourself. Handles contracts, advances, and administrative logistics. Builds relationships with promoters who will hire you for future shows.

What they DON'T do: market your music, manage your career, or sell tickets. They book the shows — you fill them.

Commission: Standard agent commission is 10% of gross booking revenue (guaranteed fee only, not merch). Some agents take 10-15%. Never pay more than 15% — that's a red flag. Never pay an agent upfront — legitimate agents work on commission only.

How to find and approach agents: (1) Research who books artists in your genre at your level. Check the credits on shows you attend. Look at similar artists' websites — agents are often listed. (2) Major booking agencies: WME, CAA, UTA, Paradigm, APA — these handle established artists. (3) Indie booking agencies: Windish Agency, High Road Touring, Billions, Arrival Artists, Mint Talent — more accessible for emerging acts. (4) Regional boutique agents: often the best entry point. Google '[your city/region] music booking agency.' (5) Ask fellow musicians who books them — warm introductions are the #1 way to get an agent.

The approach: Send a concise email: subject line: 'Booking inquiry — [Artist Name].' Include: your EPK or one-sheet, links to your music, your draw numbers (be honest), your touring history, and 2-3 specific goals ('I'm looking for support slots on [genre] tours and festival bookings'). Don't exaggerate your draw. Agents will verify, and starting a relationship with inflated numbers destroys trust.

If no agent bites yet: Keep self-booking and building your draw. Use platforms like Gigmor, Sonicbids, or Indie on the Move to find shows. Book support slots by reaching out to headliners' management directly. Every tour you self-book successfully makes you more attractive to agents.

How do I get booked at music festivals? I applied to a bunch but never hear back. Is there a secret? [Context: {"currentModule":"road","hasProject":true}]

Getting festival bookings is a numbers game AND a relationship game. Here's how the system works:

How festivals book artists: Tier 1 — Headliners: booked by the festival's talent buyer directly, usually through the artist's booking agent. These are confirmed 6-12 months in advance. Tier 2 — Mid-card: a mix of agent-pitched and application-accepted artists. Confirmed 3-6 months out. Tier 3 — Emerging/local: often sourced from open applications, showcases, and local scene curation. Confirmed 1-3 months out. As an indie artist, you're targeting Tier 3 initially, working toward Tier 2.

Application tips: (1) Apply early — most festivals have application deadlines 4-8 months before the event. Set calendar reminders. (2) Target festivals that match your genre AND size. Don't apply to Coachella as your first festival. Target: regional festivals (1,000-10,000 attendees), genre-specific festivals, city-specific festivals, college festivals. (3) Your application must include: professional press photos, a link to your best 3-5 songs (not your entire catalog), live performance video (CRITICAL — festivals need to see you can command a stage), your draw/audience evidence (social following, streaming numbers, previous show attendance), and a compelling 1-paragaph bio.

Beyond applications: (1) Showcase festivals: events like SXSW, CMJ, Americanafest, and Folk Alliance are designed for emerging artists to be seen by talent buyers. Performing at showcases puts you directly in front of the people who book major festivals. (2) Build relationships with talent buyers: follow them on social media, attend industry events, introduce yourself professionally. Don't cold-pitch aggressively — build familiarity over time. (3) Play support slots for artists who play festivals: if you open for an artist booked at a festival, their agent or manager may recommend you. (4) Regional scene building: many festivals book based on local recommendations. Be active in your local music scene and the festival's geographic community.

Maximizing your festival slot: (1) Arrive early — attend other sets, network with artists and organizers. (2) Bring your A-game — your 30-minute festival set should be your tightest, highest-energy performance. First impression matters. (3) Announce your set on social media before, during, and after. Tag the festival. (4) Have your merch game tight — the post-set merch rush is your biggest sales window. (5) Collect emails — have a signup sheet at your merch table. (6) Photograph/video everything — festival content performs well on social media.

Financial reality: Most emerging acts don't get paid much (or at all) for festival slots. Typical Tier 3 compensation: $0-$500 + free admission. The value is exposure, networking, and building your festival resume. Once you have 3-5 festival credits, you can leverage them for Tier 2 bookings with better pay ($500-$5,000).

We are routing a Midwest tour. Should we prioritize hitting major markets like Chicago and Minneapolis on weekends, even if it means zig-zagging and adding 10 hours of drive time? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

Running `optimize_tour_route` — region: Midwest, variables: weekend anchors vs drive time efficiency.

Routing optimization is a delicate balance between maximizing gross revenue and controlling logistical costs. Prioritizing major markets like Chicago and Minneapolis for Friday and Saturday nights (anchor dates) is generally the correct financial move, as weekend walk-up sales and bar guarantees in tier-1 markets are significantly higher than on a Tuesday. However, the cost of zig-zagging must be rigorously quantified.

First, calculate the hard costs of the extra 10 hours of driving. If you are in a bus getting 6 MPG, 10 extra hours (approx. 600 miles) adds roughly $400-$500 in fuel, plus potential toll roads. If you are paying a driver, you also risk hitting Department of Transportation (DOT) hours-of-service limits, which could force you to hire a relief driver or pay for an extra hotel night.

Second, factor in the human toll. Zig-zag routing increases crew and artist burnout. If the extra drive forces a 4 AM load-out and a 2 PM load-in the next day with no sleep, the performance quality drops, and crew morale plummets. If the projected weekend box office bump in Chicago exceeds the extra fuel, wages, and day-off hotel costs by at least 30%, take the routing. Otherwise, keep it linear.

Our TM wants a retainer between tours. Is this standard practice in the industry? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

Yes, paying a Tour Manager a retainer between tours is standard practice for mid-to-high tier touring artists. A retainer ensures your TM is financially stable during off-cycles and prevents them from taking another gig that might conflict with your upcoming tour dates.

Typically, a retainer is negotiated as a percentage of their active weekly road rate—often between 30% and 50%. In exchange for this retainer, the TM does not just sit idle. They are actively handling the off-cycle workload: advancing the next run of shows, reconciling tour accounting, booking flights and hotels, and managing pre-production logistics.

If you do not pay a retainer, your TM is a freelancer. They have every right to book other tours to pay their bills, meaning you may have to scramble to find and train a new TM right before your next tour. A retainer is an investment in the consistency and professionalism of your touring operation.

Our hospitality rider asks for venue catering. Should we switch to asking for a buyout instead? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

Switching your hospitality rider to request a buyout instead of venue catering is often the preferred move for touring bands at the club and theater level. A buyout is a cash payment provided by the promoter (usually $20 to $30 per traveling member) in lieu of a hot meal.

The primary advantage of a buyout is flexibility. Venue catering can be highly inconsistent; a promoter's idea of a 'hot meal' might be a stack of lukewarm pizzas that don't accommodate your bass player's gluten allergy or your tour manager's vegan diet. With cash in hand, your crew can eat exactly what they want, when they want it—whether that's finding a local restaurant before soundcheck or hoarding the cash to save money.

When updating your rider, explicitly state your terms: 'Purchaser agrees to provide a hot, healthy meal for [X] traveling personnel. If catering cannot be provided, a cash buyout of $25 per head ($[Total] total) must be paid to the Tour Manager at load-in.'

A professional day sheet keeps everyone aligned and prevents missed cues. Here's the standard flow for a club show:

**The Day Sheet (200-500 Cap Venue):**

| Time | Activity | Notes |
|------|----------|-------|
| 2:00 PM | Load-in | Arrive, unload gear, meet venue contact |
| 2:30 PM | Stage setup | Set up backline, run cables, position monitors |
| 3:00 PM | Sound check (headliner) | Headliner checks first (they set stage positions) |
| 3:45 PM | Sound check (support) | Opener checks after headliner |
| 4:30 PM | Dinner / downtime | Venue may provide buyout ($15-25/person) or catering |
| 6:30 PM | Doors open | FOH music starts, merch table set up |
| 7:30 PM | Support set | Opener plays 30-45 min |
| 8:15 PM | Changeover | 15-20 min to swap gear |
| 8:30 PM | Headliner set | 60-90 min depending on deal |
| 10:00 PM | Load-out | Pack up, clear stage within 30-60 min |
| 10:30 PM | Settlement | Settle with venue: get paid, reconcile merch, sign off |

**Critical Day-Of Checklist:**
- [ ] Venue advance confirmed (load-in time, parking, gear access)
- [ ] Merch counted and displayed before doors
- [ ] Set list finalized and given to sound engineer
- [ ] Guest list submitted to box office
- [ ] Drink tickets / meal buyout collected
- [ ] Stage plot/tech rider verifiable with house engineer
- [ ] Settlement completed and documented before leaving

**Independent Artist Must-Do:**
- ALWAYS settle the night of the show. Never leave without getting paid or documenting the agreement. Get a settlement sheet signed by the venue.
- Take photos of the merch count post-show for your records.
- Thank the sound engineer and venue staff. They remember who's professional.

A label says they'll provide tour support money. Is that worth signing for? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true,"artistProfile":{"goal":"fully-independent","stage":"developing","genre":"indie-rock"}}]

Tour support sounds generous — but understand the economics before you sign:

**What Tour Support Actually Is:**
- The label covers your touring losses (when tour costs exceed tour income)
- Typical range: $500-5,000+ per show for developing artists
- This money is nearly always RECOUPABLE — it's an advance against your future royalties

**The Math:**
- Label provides $30,000 tour support for a 20-date tour = $1,500/show subsidy
- That $30,000 goes on your recoupment balance
- With a 15% artist royalty rate, you need to generate $200,000 in revenue before that tour support is 'paid off'
- Meanwhile, the label earns from day one through their 85% share

**What an Independent Tour Looks Like:**
- You eat the losses upfront (van, gas, hotels, food)
- A 10-date club tour might cost $3,000-7,000 out of pocket
- But you keep 100% of merch income (potentially $2,000-5,000+)
- And you keep 100% of door/guarantee income
- Net loss on a first indie tour: often $0-3,000 — a fraction of label tour support

**The Independent Advantage:**
- You lose less real money by touring independently than by receiving recoupable tour support
- You build audience without accumulating debt
- You can tour at YOUR pace, in YOUR markets, on YOUR schedule

**When Label Tour Support Makes Sense:**
- They're opening for a major artist (exposure you can't get independently)
- The support is NON-recoupable (rare but negotiate for it)
- The label's distribution and marketing push makes the tour significantly more profitable

I got an offer to play 3 shows in the UK. I've never toured internationally. What do I need to know about visas, bringing gear, and getting paid overseas? [Context: {"currentModule":"road","hasProject":true}]

International touring is exciting but has serious logistical and legal requirements. Showing up without the right paperwork can get you detained, deported, and banned from future entry. Here's the UK-specific checklist:

Visas/Work Permits: As a US citizen performing commercially in the UK, you need a Temporary Worker — Creative and Sporting (T5) visa. Cost: approximately £298 for the application + £624 Immigration Health Surcharge. You need a Certificate of Sponsorship from a UK-based sponsor (typically the promoter, venue, or a sponsorship agency). Processing time: 3-8 weeks. Apply early. Alternative: If your 3 shows are truly 'incidental' to another purpose and you're not being paid in the UK, you MAY qualify under Standard Visitor rules — but this is risky and HMRC can challenge it.

Bringing Gear: ATA Carnet (pronounced car-NAY): This is an international customs document that lets you temporarily import professional equipment (instruments, PA equipment, merch) without paying import duties or taxes. Apply through the US Council for International Business (uscib.org). Cost: $200-$400+ depending on the value of your gear. Processing: 1-2 weeks.

Getting Paid: UK promoters will likely pay in GBP (British Pounds). Open a Wise (formerly TransferWise) multi-currency account before departure. Wise gives you local UK bank details and converts at near-market rates (0.5-1% fee vs 3-5% at a traditional bank). Withholding tax: The UK may withhold 15-20% of your performance fees for tax purposes. You can potentially claim this back under the US-UK tax treaty (form DT-Individual). Keep all contracts, invoices, and payment receipts for your US tax return — you can claim foreign tax credits.

Logistics: Airlines and instruments: Know the airline's instrument policy. Most allow a guitar in the cabin if it fits in the overhead bin. Check in advance and carry your instrument policy printout. British electrical outlets use Type G (3-prong). Bring voltage converters for US equipment. UK is left-hand traffic — factor this into driving plans.

Insurance: Tour insurance covering equipment, liability, and cancellation. This is NOT optional — one stolen guitar can cost more than the entire tour earns.

Budget realistically: International touring almost always loses money on the first trip. The goal is market building, not profit. Plan to break even and consider anything above that a bonus.

We had to cancel a tour leg due to illness, but we signed a hotel contract with a strict 80% attrition clause. How do we get out of paying for empty rooms? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

Running `analyze_contract` — reviewing hotel attrition clauses and force majeure applications.

Handling a strict attrition clause after a cancellation requires immediate communication and a thorough review of your hotel contract's 'Force Majeure' or 'Act of God' provisions. An 80% attrition clause means you are legally obligated to pay for 80% of the contracted room block revenue, even if no one shows up. However, if the cancellation was due to a severe, documented illness (like a hospitalization or a highly contagious disease affecting the artist), you may be able to invoke Force Majeure to terminate the agreement without liability.

First, gather all medical documentation and immediately notify the hotel's Director of Sales in writing that the tour leg is canceled due to a medical emergency. Explain that the artist's inability to perform makes the travel impossible. If the hotel pushes back and claims the illness does not qualify as a Force Majeure event, your next step is to negotiate a mitigation strategy. Hotels have a legal duty to mitigate damages, meaning they must try to resell your canceled rooms to the general public.

Ask the hotel to release the rooms back into their general inventory immediately. If they successfully book those rooms to other guests, they cannot double-charge you for the attrition penalty. Alternatively, you can negotiate to pay a reduced cancellation fee or agree to rebook the same property when the tour is rescheduled later in the year, applying your penalty payment as a deposit toward the future stay.

We have a 9-hour drive between shows with no day off. Do we drive overnight? [Context: {"currentModule":"road"}]

Nine-hour drive with no day off is a critical safety decision. My protocol is clear: never recommend overnight drives after a show.

The math: Show ends 11 PM, load-out 12:30 AM, departure 1 AM, arrival 10 AM. That's 9 hours of driving with a fatigued crew who just performed. This is how accidents happen.

Safe Alternatives:
1. Split drive: Leave morning after show, drive 5 hours, stop at midpoint hotel, drive remaining 4 hours next morning. Arrive afternoon for load-in.
2. Early departure: If load-out finishes by midnight, everyone sleeps at hotel, depart 4 AM for 1 PM arrival.
3. Dual drivers: If you MUST drive overnight, minimum 2 qualified drivers rotating every 2.5 hours. The non-driving crew member stays awake as the 'co-pilot.'
4. DOT regulations: If using a tour bus with a professional driver, DOT limits 10 hours of driving after 8 consecutive hours off. They cannot legally drive 9 hours after loading out at midnight.

A venue told me they'd give me a 'door deal' instead of a guarantee. Another venue offered a $300 guarantee. Which is better? [Context: {"currentModule":"road","hasProject":true}]

This depends entirely on how many people you can draw. Here's the breakdown:

Guarantee: the venue pays you a fixed amount regardless of attendance. $300 guarantee = you get $300 whether 5 or 500 people show up. Best for: artists unsure about their draw in a specific market. Provides financial certainty for tour budgeting. Downside: if you draw well, you might have earned more on a door deal.

Door deal: you receive a percentage of ticket revenue from the door. Common structures: 100% of the door after expenses (sound engineer, door person). 80/20 split (you get 80%, venue keeps 20%). 70/30 split. Example: $10 tickets × 50 people = $500 gross. Venue deducts $100 for sound/door. You receive 80% of $400 = $320. Best for: artists with a proven draw. Higher upside but higher risk.

Guarantee PLUS: the best deal — a guaranteed minimum PLUS a percentage of ticket sales above a threshold. Example: $300 guarantee + 80% of door revenue above $500. If you sell $800 in tickets: you get $300 + 80% of ($800 - $500) = $300 + $240 = $540. This protects your downside while rewarding a strong draw.

Tiered deals: some venues offer escalating splits. 0-50 tickets: 100% to venue (they cover costs). 51-100 tickets: 80/20 to artist. 101+: 85/15 to artist.

Decision framework: If you CAN'T reliably draw 30+ people in this market: take the guarantee. A guaranteed $300 beats a potential door deal that yields $150 if only 20 people show up. If you CAN reliably draw 50+ people: take the door deal or negotiate guarantee-plus. 50 people × $12 ticket × 80% = $480 — significantly more than a $300 guarantee. In a new market (first time playing there): always take the guarantee. You have no data on your draw. In your home market: always take the door deal or guarantee-plus. You know your draw.

Negotiation tips: If offered a $200 guarantee and you believe you can draw 40 people: counter with: '$200 guarantee, OR 80% of the door — whichever is higher.' This gives you downside protection with upside potential. Always ask: what's the ticket price, what are the deductions from gross, and on what number are we splitting?

The most critical document you need is the final ticket manifest generated directly from the primary ticketing system (like Ticketmaster or AXS). Never accept a manually typed spreadsheet as proof of sales. You will cross-check the manifest against the 'drop count'—the physical or scanned count of tickets actually used at the door—to account for deadwood (unsold tickets) and comps.

Next, review the deduction sheet. You need to calculate the Gross Ticket Receipts and then subtract approved taxes, facility fees, and ASCAP/BMI deductions to find the Net Ticket Receipts. If your deal is a guarantee versus a percentage (e.g., 85% of Net after documented expenses), you must scrutinize every line item in the promoter's expense report. Demand receipts for variable costs like local catering, runner vans, or extra security.

Finally, ensure your guarantee and any negotiated walkout bonuses are paid out correctly. Walk away with signed copies of the settlement sheet, the final box office statement, and the cash or wire confirmation. If anything looks incorrect, note the dispute in writing on the settlement sheet before signing.

The hotel contract for our tour block has an 'attrition clause' at 80%. What does this mean if our routing changes? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

An attrition clause of 80% means your tour is financially responsible for paying for at least 80% of the room nights you blocked, regardless of whether you actually use them. If you blocked 10 rooms for the night, the hotel requires you to pay for 8 of them. If your routing changes and you cancel the block entirely past the penalty date, you owe the hotel the revenue for those 8 rooms.

To protect yourself, you must negotiate a 'cut-off date' alongside the attrition clause. The cut-off date (usually 21 to 30 days prior to arrival) is the deadline by which you can release unbooked rooms back into the hotel's general inventory without facing any financial penalty. 

Always have your Tour Manager or travel coordinator set calendar alerts 48 hours before every cut-off date on the tour. This allows you to review the routing, drop the rooms you don't need, and avoid triggering the 80% attrition penalty.

Where should I put day offs on a 14-date tour? I don't want to waste them in boring cities. [Context: {"currentModule":"road"}]

Day-off strategy is an art:

1. NEVER more than 4 shows in a row without a day off. Fatigue compounds — show 5 without rest will be your worst show.

2. Place days off AFTER the longest drive. If you have a brutal 8-hour drive, the day off absorbs it. You drive during the day and have the evening to rest.

3. Fun cities for days off: Nashville, Austin, New Orleans, Portland, Denver. Cities where the crew can actually enjoy themselves and recharge.

4. Laundry stops: Every day off needs access to laundry. 14 days of stage clothes in a van is a biohazard.

5. Maintenance days: Use one day off for vehicle maintenance check, restock supplies, and data entry (settle previous shows, update budget).

For a 14-date tour: 3 shows on, 1 off, 4 shows on, 1 off, 4 shows on, 1 off, 3 shows on = 14 shows + 3 days off = 17 touring days.

We have a $10k guarantee vs 85% of net box office receipts (NBOR) deal. The gross is $25k, taxes are 8%, and documented expenses are $6k. Can you walk me through the settlement math? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

Running `calculate_settlement` — Deal: $10k vs 85% NBOR. Gross: $25k, Tax: 8%, Expenses: $6k.

Let's walk through the exact settlement math to determine your final walkout potential. First, we need to back out the 8% tax from the Gross to find the Net Ticket Sales. You do this by dividing the Gross by 1.08 (not by multiplying by 0.92, which is a common mistake). $25,000 / 1.08 = $23,148.15. This is your Net Gross.

Next, we subtract the documented show expenses from the Net Gross to find the Net Box Office Receipts (NBOR). $23,148.15 minus $6,000 equals $17,148.15. This NBOR is the pool of money that gets split between the artist and the promoter.

Now, calculate your 85% cut of the NBOR. 85% of $17,148.15 is $14,575.93. Since your deal is a "versus" deal, you compare this number to your guarantee and take whichever is higher. Since your 85% cut ($14,575.93) is greater than your guarantee ($10,000), you are in "percentage" or "overage." Your final walkout for the night should be $14,575.93.

**IMPORTANT: Start this process NOW (4-6 months before travel).**

**🇬🇧 United Kingdom — Temporary Worker Creative (Tier 5):**
Post-Brexit, US musicians need a Tier 5 Creative Worker visa to perform paid shows in the UK.

1. **Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS):** Your UK promoter/venue must be a licensed sponsor. They apply for a CoS on your behalf.
2. **Visa Application:** You apply at a UK visa office (VFS Global) with:
   - Completed online application
   - Certificate of Sponsorship reference number
   - Valid passport (6+ months validity)
   - Proof of funds (bank statements showing ~£1,270 available)
   - Itinerary with venue confirmations
   - Evidence of career (press, streaming stats, previous tour history)
3. **Processing time:** 3-6 weeks (standard) or 5 days (fast-track, ~£500 extra)
4. **Cost:** £298 visa fee + £235 Immigration Health Surcharge

**🇩🇪 Germany (Schengen Zone):**
Good news: US citizens can perform in Germany for up to 90 days within a 180-day period WITHOUT a visa for performances (under the Schengen visa waiver). However:

1. **Short stay = no visa needed** for performances ✅
2. **BUT:** You may need a work notification (Anzeigepflicht) depending on the federal state. Your promoter should handle this.
3. **Tax implications:** Germany withholds tax on artist payments (typically 15-20%). You can often reclaim this under the US-Germany tax treaty. Keep all receipts.

**Carnet / Equipment:**
If you're bringing gear across borders, you may need an ATA Carnet (essentially a passport for your equipment). Without it, customs can charge import duties.

**Currency & Banking:**
Get a no-foreign-transaction-fee card (Charles Schwab, Wise) BEFORE you leave. ATM withdrawals with a regular US bank card cost $5-7 per withdrawal + poor exchange rates.

How do we handle per diems for our 4-person crew? Should we give them cash daily or add it to their weekly paycheck? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

Running `calculate_crew_rates` — managing per diem distribution and touring cash flow.

Per diems (PDs) are daily cash allowances provided to the band and crew to cover meals and incidental expenses while on the road. The industry standard for touring per diems ranges from $30 to $50 per day, depending on whether the venue is providing a buyout or catering. For a 4-person crew, at $40 a day, you are looking at $160 in daily cash outlay.

It is highly recommended to distribute per diems in cash on a daily or weekly basis while on the tour, rather than adding them to the crew's post-tour paycheck. The entire purpose of a per diem is to ensure your crew has liquid funds to feed themselves at truck stops, coffee shops, or venues without having to dip into their personal savings. Many Tour Managers prefer to hand out a week's worth of PDs in cash on the first day of the touring week (e.g., $280 per person) in small envelopes, which reduces the daily administrative burden of tracking down an ATM.

If you choose to distribute PDs digitally (via Venmo or Zelle), be aware that this can complicate accounting. Cash PDs are generally considered non-taxable reimbursements by the IRS as long as they fall under the federal standard rate, but if you roll them into a formal payroll check, they may be subject to payroll taxes unless strictly itemized. Stick to cash envelopes or weekly digital transfers, and always have the crew sign a PD receipt sheet to maintain pristine accounting for your tour settlement.

I'm putting together a 12-city tour. How do I figure out the best route? I don't want to be driving 10 hours between shows. [Context: {"currentModule":"road","hasProject":true}]

Tour routing is logistics meets math meets strategy. Bad routing is the #1 reason indie tours lose money. Here's how to plan efficiently:

The golden rules: (1) Maximum drive time between shows: 4-5 hours. Anything over 6 hours is punishing and expensive. (2) Never backtrack — always move in one direction (loop or linear). (3) Day-off placement: after the longest drives, not in the cheapest cities. (4) Start and end near home to minimize empty-leg driving.

Routing methods: Linear route: start at city A, drive in one direction to city L, fly/drive home. Example: NYC → Philly → DC → Richmond → Charlotte → Atlanta → Nashville → Louisville → Columbus → Pittsburgh → NYC (Northeast-to-Southeast loop). Cluster routing: group nearby cities together. Play 3-4 shows in a tight geographic cluster, then drive to the next cluster. Example: Cluster 1 (Northeast): NYC, Philly, DC, Baltimore — all within 2-3 hour drives. Cluster 2 (Southeast): Richmond, Raleigh, Charlotte, Atlanta — drives of 2-4 hours. One longer drive (4-5 hours) connects the clusters.

Tools for routing: Google Maps multi-stop route planner. RouteXL (optimizes multi-stop driving routes). Bandzoogle or Indie on the Move (shows you venues by city). Master Tour (professional tour management app, $15/month).

Day-off strategy: You need days off — touring without rest leads to illness, vocal fatigue, and burnout. Schedule 1 day off every 3-4 shows. Time day offs to coincide with: longer drives (arrive the day before, rest, play the next night), cities with friends/family (free accommodation on your day off), cities with cultural interest (a day off in Nashville is better than a day off on the interstate).

Financial routing considerations: Gas cost per mile: ~$0.25-$0.40 for a van. A 300-mile drive = $75-$120 in gas. Calculate total mileage for your proposed route BEFORE booking. Compare: Route A (12 shows, 3,200 total miles) vs Route B (12 shows, 4,800 total miles). Route B costs $400-$640 MORE in gas alone + additional wear on the vehicle.

Pro tip: Book your anchor shows first (the cities where you have the strongest draw or the best guarantee). Then fill in shows between anchor dates. It's easier to book a Tuesday in a random city when you can tell the venue: 'I'm playing [respected venue] in [nearby city] on Monday and [another venue] on Thursday — I need a Tuesday stop between them.'

I'm selling merch at my shows but the revenue is inconsistent — sometimes great, sometimes almost nothing. How do I optimize merch sales at shows? [Context: {"currentModule":"touring"}]

Inconsistent merch revenue is usually a display/timing/pitch problem, not a product problem.

**The Five Drivers of Live Merch Revenue:**

**1. Placement:**
Merch table as close to the stage exit as possible — never at the back near the bar. Fans buying merch do so in the 15-minute post-show emotional window. If the table is hard to find, you lose the sale.

**2. Post-Show Window:**
The best merch sales happen when you are AT the table after your set. Your presence is the final conversion factor. If you disappear after the show, revenue drops significantly. Block 30–45 minutes after your set exclusively for the merch table — no exceptions.

**3. From Stage:**

We have extensive low-severity block cracking, moderate raveling, and average rut depths of 0.45 inches. Structural capacity (FWD testing) is adequate. Given a PCI of 72 with adequate structural capacity, this pavement is an excellent candidate for preservation rather than rehabilitation. However, the rut depth of 0.45 inches is the critical deciding factor here. 

A standard chip seal will effectively seal the low-severity block cracking and arrest the moderate raveling, but it has zero rut-filling capability. Applying a chip seal over 0.45-inch ruts will simply mirror the ruts and cause water to pond, leading to stripping or hydroplaning.

Micro-surfacing is highly effective at rut filling (using a specialized rut box) and will resolve the raveling. However, micro-surfacing is a rigid, cold-applied treatment. It is notoriously poor at mitigating reflective cracking; the block cracking will reflect through a micro-surface within 12 to 18 months.

The optimal solution is the Ultra-Thin Bonded Wearing Course (UTBWC). The UTBWC uses a heavy application of polymer-modified emulsion membrane applied immediately ahead of a hot, open- or gap-graded asphalt mix. The heavy emulsion membrane will seal the block cracking and prevent water intrusion, while the structural nature of the hot mix will effectively fill the 0.45-inch ruts and cure the raveling. While more expensive than micro-surfacing, UTBWC is the only option among the three that simultaneously addresses the rutting, seals the block cracking, and restores the surface friction without requiring milling.

How does a venue settlement actually work? I've never done a box office split before. [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

[Mode A: Curriculum] Venue settlement is the process of reconciling the money generated by ticket sales against the costs of putting on the show. It typically happens at the end of the night with the promoter or venue manager. We start with the Gross Box Office Receipts (GBOR), which is the total money collected from all ticket tiers before any taxes or fees are removed.

From the GBOR, the venue will deduct taxes (like state sales tax) and any agreed-upon facility fees to reach the Net Gross. Next, we look at the show expenses. If you're on a Versus deal (e.g., $2,000 guarantee vs. 80% of net after expenses), the venue deducts their documented expenses (sound engineer, security, marketing, ASCAP/BMI fees) from the Net Gross to find the Walkout Potential.

At settlement, you must ask to see the 'drop count' (the actual number of scanned tickets) to verify the promoter's numbers. Never accept a settlement sheet without verifying the math against your contract. If you have the settlement sheet from last night, upload it, and we'll walk through the deductions line by line.

I toured 15 states last year and made about $120K from performances. My accountant says I might have tax issues in multiple states. What is 'tax nexus' for touring musicians? [Context: {"currentModule":"touring"}]

Your accountant is correct — multi-state touring creates multi-state tax obligations that many touring artists discover only when they receive state tax notices years later.

**What is Tax Nexus?**
Nexus means you have sufficient presence in a state to trigger a tax filing obligation. For touring musicians, physical presence (performing in that state) creates nexus in most states. Even one show can create a filing obligation.

**The Touring Musician's State Tax Reality:**
- You owe state income tax to each state where you earned performance income
- You file as a 'nonresident' in each state
- You get a credit on your home state return to avoid double taxation — but only if you actually FILE the returns in each state

**The High-Stakes States:**
- **California**: Top marginal rate 13.3%. Withholds 7% at source from venue payments to nonresident performers on contracts over $1,500. If venues didn't withhold and you didn't file, you may owe CA back taxes + penalties.
- **New York**: Files aggressively against nonresident touring income. NYC adds a city tax layer on top of state tax.
- **Pennsylvania**: Has its own nonresident entertainer tax withholding requirement.
- **Tennessee, Texas, Florida, Washington**: No income tax — shows here create no income tax obligation.

**At $120K across 15 states:**
Your blended state tax exposure is potentially $8,000–$15,000 in state taxes owed (minus credits). Whether you have CA or NY shows significantly changes this number.

Your accountant needs your complete touring income breakdown by state — promoter settlement sheets from each show establish this. Do you have those records?

After almost getting burned by a tour cancellation, I want to negotiate better protection clauses in all my future promoter contracts. What specific force majeure language, deposit structure, and mutual cancellation provisions should I ask for to protect against cancellation scenarios from both sides? [Context: {"currentModule":"touring","artistProfile":{"goal":"fully-independent","stage":"developing","genre":"country"}}]

Strong contract language is your best protection. Here are the specific clauses to negotiate.

**1. Force Majeure Definition (Broaden the Triggers)**
Standard language: 'Acts of God, war, natural disaster, government prohibition'
Push for: 'Acts of God, war, natural disaster, government prohibition, civil unrest, epidemic or pandemic, fire, flood, labor dispute, failure or insolvency of any material supplier or vendor engaged by Artist or Promoter, or any other cause beyond the reasonable control of the affected party'

The addition of 'failure or insolvency of any material supplier or vendor' is the specific protection you lacked. Most promoters will accept this because it protects BOTH sides (if their venue has a supplier failure, they're protected too).

**2. Force Majeure Consequences — Mutual Excuse**
Standard promoter contracts often say force majeure excuses the artist's performance but still requires deposit refund. Push for: 'In the event of force majeure as defined herein, both parties shall be excused from performance and neither party shall owe any financial obligation to the other. Artist shall retain any deposits received prior to the force majeure event.'

**3. Deposit Structure — Protect Against Artist Liability**
Structure deposits to minimize your exposure for cancellation:
- Non-refundable deposit language from PROMOTER perspective: 'Artist deposit is non-refundable in the event of Promoter cancellation'
- Artist cancellation provision: 'In the event of Artist cancellation for reasons other than force majeure, with more than [60] days notice, Promoter shall retain deposit as liquidated damages and Artist shall have no further liability. With less than [60] days notice, Artist shall refund deposit and pay Promoter's documented out-of-pocket costs not to exceed $[X].'

The $[X] cap is critical — without a cap, 'actual damages' for a promoter can be enormous if they've run a full marketing campaign.

**4. Cancellation Notice Windows**
Establish clear windows with different consequences:
- 90+ days before show: Promoter retains deposit only; Artist owes nothing additional
- 30-90 days: Promoter retains deposit + Artist pays documented marketing costs (capped at $5,000)
- <30 days: Promoter retains deposit + Artist pays documented costs + a reasonable penalty (negotiate a specific dollar amount, not 'all damages')

**5. Promoter Cancellation Provisions (Often Forgotten)**
Artists focus on protecting against their own cancellation but forget to protect against PROMOTER cancellation:
'In the event Promoter cancels or postpones this engagement, Promoter shall pay Artist the full contracted guarantee within 5 business days of cancellation notice, regardless of the reason for cancellation.'
This protects you from promoters who cancel shows at the last minute citing financial difficulties.

**6. Production Contingency Language**
Given your specific experience: 'Artist's performance obligation is contingent upon Artist securing production services meeting industry technical rider requirements. In the event production services are unavailable through no fault of Artist, such unavailability shall constitute force majeure.'

Running `analyze_festival_offer` — evaluating festival radius clauses and negotiation strategies.

A 300-mile, 90-day radius clause is standard for major tier-one festivals like Lollapalooza. The festival promoter (C3 Presents/Live Nation) is paying you a premium guarantee, and in exchange, they want exclusivity. They don't want fans in Milwaukee, Indianapolis, or Detroit skipping the festival because they know they can see you play a cheaper club show in their hometown a month later. Technically, yes, this clause prohibits you from playing any public, ticketed shows within that radius for 90 days before and after the festival.

However, radius clauses are almost always negotiable, especially for mid-tier or emerging artists who rely on continuous touring to survive. Your booking agent needs to push back during the offer phase. The standard strategy is to request 'carve-outs' for specific routing needs. For example, you can ask for permission to play a club show in Detroit 60 days prior, arguing that it's a different market that won't cannibalize Chicago festival ticket sales.

Additionally, festivals often waive the radius clause for official 'aftershows' or pre-parties sanctioned by the festival itself. If the promoter refuses to budge on the radius, you must calculate the 'opportunity cost.' If the Lollapalooza guarantee is $15,000, but the radius clause forces you to cancel $25,000 worth of regional club dates, you need to demand a higher festival guarantee to offset the lost touring revenue.

I just got booked for my first headlining show at a real venue. What should I expect on the day of the show? What's sound check like? [Context: {"currentModule":"road","hasProject":true}]

Congratulations on your first headline! Here's the complete day-of-show timeline so nothing catches you by surprise:

Pre-show (do these BEFORE show day): Confirm: load-in time, soundcheck time, set time, and set length with the venue/promoter. Send your stage plot and input list to the venue's sound engineer at least 3-5 days before the show. A stage plot shows where each performer stands on stage and what equipment they need. An input list details every microphone, DI, and monitor channel your band needs. Confirm: is backline provided (amps, drums) or do you bring everything? Confirm: guest list capacity and process.

Day-of timeline: LOAD-IN (typically 4-6 hours before doors): arrive at the venue. Park at the loading dock or designated area. Bring all equipment inside and set it up on stage. This includes: instruments, pedalboards, merch (set up your merch table), and any props or visual elements. Introduce yourself to the venue staff — sound engineer, stage manager, bar staff, door person.

SOUNDCHECK (typically 3-5 hours before doors): Each band/artist gets a soundcheck slot (15-45 minutes depending on the lineup). Headliner typically soundchecks FIRST (you get the most time) or LAST (you play right after checking). During soundcheck: play parts of 2-3 songs (not your full set). The sound engineer adjusts your levels in the main speakers (front of house / FOH). The sound engineer adjusts your monitor mix (what YOU hear on stage). Communicate clearly: 'Can I get more vocals in my monitor?' 'The guitar is too loud.' 'I need reverb on the vocal.' Play your LOUDEST and QUIETEST songs so the engineer knows your dynamic range.

PRE-SHOW (1-2 hours before doors): doors open. Eat dinner (hopefully the venue provides a meal — check your contract/rider). Get your merch table organized. Price signs visible, Square/cash ready. Run through your setlist one more time mentally. Warm up your voice/instruments. Double-check your tuning after soundcheck (temperature changes can shift tuning).

SHOWTIME: Opening acts play their sets. You go on at your scheduled set time (DO NOT BE LATE taking the stage). Play your set. Common set lengths: local headliner: 45-60 minutes. Touring headliner: 60-90 minutes. Leave 2-3 songs' worth of energy for an encore if the crowd demands it.

POST-SHOW: Immediately go to your merch table — the post-show rush is your highest-sales window. Thank fans, take photos, sign things. Load out your equipment within the venue's required timeframe (usually within 30-60 minutes of your set ending). Collect your payment from the venue (get it in cash or check THAT NIGHT if possible — don't leave without being paid). Thank the sound engineer and venue staff.

The promoter said we are doing a 'versus deal' tonight. What does that mean for my settlement? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

[Mode A: Curriculum] A 'versus deal' (often written as 'Guarantee vs. Percentage') means you will be paid either a flat guaranteed amount OR a percentage of the Net Box Office Receipts (NBOR) after expenses—whichever number is higher.

At settlement, the venue will calculate the gross ticket sales, then deduct taxes, facility fees, and approved show expenses (like local marketing, ASCAP/BMI blanket licenses, and sometimes catering or support act buyouts). The remaining amount is the net.

If your guarantee is $1,000, and your percentage split (say, 85% of net) calculates out to $1,500, you walk away with $1,500. If the room is empty and your percentage is only $400, you still walk away with your $1,000 guarantee. Always review the itemized deductions on the settlement sheet before signing off at the end of the night.

Do I need a booking agent? I've been booking my own shows but it's exhausting. When is the right time to get one and how do I find them? [Context: {"currentModule":"road","hasProject":true}]

A booking agent takes over the work of securing and negotiating live performance deals. Here's when it makes sense and how to find one:

When do you NEED one? You're ready for a booking agent when: (1) You can consistently draw 50-100+ people to your own shows in your home market. (2) You're playing 15-20+ shows per year. (3) You're turning down show offers because you can't manage the volume. (4) You want to expand beyond your region. If you're playing 5-10 shows a year to 20 people, an agent won't take you on — there's not enough commission to justify their time.

What agents do: Negotiate guarantees and deal terms with venues/promoters. Route tours efficiently (logistics matter — an agent who books a show in Boston on Monday and Atlanta on Tuesday is a bad agent). Secure festival slots, support slots for larger acts, and private events. Handle contracts, riders, and settlement disputes.

What agents DON'T do: They don't promote your shows (that's on you and the promoter). They don't manage your career (that's a manager). They don't handle merch, travel, or production.

Commission: Standard is 10-15% of your performance fee (gross guarantee or net door income). 10% is ideal. 15% is acceptable. Above 15% — negotiate down.

How to find an agent: (1) Look at who books artists similar to you in your genre and market size. Check artist websites for 'booking' contact info. (2) Attend industry conferences: Folk Alliance, SXSW, Americana Fest, CMJ. (3) Showcase: play curated showcases where agents are in the audience. (4) Ask other artists in your scene for recommendations. (5) Agencies for emerging indie artists: Arrival Artists, Paradigm (now Wasserman but has indie rosters), Partisan Group, Madison House.

Before approaching an agent: Have a one-sheet ready (bio, photo, streaming stats, press quotes, draw numbers by market). Have a live video (full song, good audio/video quality). Have your streaming and social metrics current.

Until you're ready, keep booking yourself. The skillset of self-booking (negotiating, advancing, routing) will make you a much better client when you finally get an agent.

I am evaluating the drainage geometry for a 4-lane undivided highway curve (radius 2,000 ft) in a region with a 100-year design rainfall intensity of 6 in/hr. The pavement is dense-graded asphalt. To mitigate dynamic hydroplaning in the outermost lanes, how do I calculate and optimize the resultant flow path length and water film thickness using the Gallaway or similar empirical models? [Context: {"lanes":4,"radius_ft":2000,"rainfall_intensity_in_hr":6,"pavement_type":"Dense-graded asphalt"}]

To mitigate dynamic hydroplaning on a 4-lane curve with intense rainfall (6 in/hr), you must minimize the Water Film Thickness (WFT). The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) and the Gallaway empirical model dictate that hydroplaning risk spikes when WFT exceeds 0.15 inches (4 mm).

1. Resultant Flow Path: On a superelevated curve, water does not flow straight across the lanes; it flows diagonally. The resultant slope (Sr) is the vector sum of the cross slope (Sx) and the longitudinal grade (Sl): Sr = √(Sx² + Sl²). The resultant flow path length (Lr) increases significantly on multi-lane facilities. Lr = W * (Sr / Sx), where W is the total pavement width. Because this is a 4-lane undivided section on a curve, water from the high side must cross all 4 lanes, creating a massive Lr and thick WFT in the lowest lane.

2. Optimization Strategy: To reduce WFT via the Gallaway formula (WFT = f(Lr, rainfall intensity, Sr, mean texture depth)), you cannot easily change the rainfall or the Lr without changing the lane count. Therefore, you must increase the cross slope (Sx) to accelerate runoff. Given the 2,000 ft radius, utilize a steeper superelevation rate (e.g., 6% to 8%) rather than a minimum rate. Ensure the longitudinal grade (Sl) is minimized through the curve to keep the flow path as perpendicular to the roadway as possible, reducing Lr. Finally, because dense-graded asphalt has a low mean texture depth (MTD), strongly consider specifying a porous friction course (PFC) or Open-Graded Friction Course (OGFC) for this curve. An OGFC significantly increases macrotexture and allows water to flow internally, drastically reducing the effective surface WFT.

I'm an American artist planning shows in Europe. Beyond visas, what logistics do I need to plan for? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true,"artistProfile":{"goal":"fully-independent","stage":"developing","genre":"electronic"}}]

International touring adds significant complexity. Here's the full logistics checklist beyond visas:

**Equipment & Power:**
- Europe uses 220-240V / 50Hz (US is 120V / 60Hz). Bring VOLTAGE CONVERTERS, not just plug adapters.
- Verify all your gear is dual-voltage (check the label: 'Input: 100-240V' = safe. '120V only' = needs converter).
- ATA carnet: A 'passport for gear.' Required to temporarily import equipment into many countries without paying import duties. Apply via US Council for International Business. Process takes 2-3 weeks.

**Financial:**
- Currency: Euro zone vs UK (GBP) vs Scandinavia (SEK/NOK/DKK). Have a multi-currency bank account or card (Wise, Revolut).
- Payment: Some European venues pay in cash (EUR). Some wire after the show. Confirm payment method and currency in advance.
- Withholding tax: Many European countries withhold 15-30% tax on performance income from foreign artists. Some have double-taxation treaties with the US that reduce this. File for treaty benefits BEFORE the tour.

**Travel:**
- Schengen area: 90 days max within any 180-day period for US passport holders. Plan your tour within this window.
- Rail passes: European trains are often faster than flying between cities (London-Paris, Amsterdam-Brussels, etc.).
- Rental vehicles: International driving permits required in some countries. Rental insurance differs from US.

**Communication:**
- International phone plan or eSIM (Airalo is popular for touring musicians)
- Wi-Fi at venues is unreliable. Have your own data solution.

**Health:**
- Travel insurance with medical coverage is essential. US health insurance typically doesn't cover Europe.
- Bring prescriptions in original bottles with a letter from your doctor.

Running `calculate_tour_budget` — structuring dual-role TM/FOH compensation for club circuits.

When hiring a dual-role TM/FOH (Tour Manager and Front of House engineer), you should almost always offer a weekly rate rather than a per-show rate. A Tour Manager's job doesn't stop on days off; they are advancing upcoming shows, advancing hotels, doing accounting, and wrangling the band. If you pay them per-show, they are essentially working for free on travel and off days, which leads to rapid burnout and resentment. A weekly rate guarantees their income and acknowledges the 24/7 nature of the TM role.

For a club tour (500 to 1,500 capacity rooms) in the current touring economy, a standard weekly rate for a competent, experienced TM/FOH ranges from $1,800 to $2,500 per week, plus per diems and a private hotel room. The exact number depends on the complexity of your production (are they mixing 16 channels or 48?) and the intensity of the routing.

If the tour is very short (e.g., a 4-day weekend run), you can negotiate a day rate instead. A standard day rate for this dual role is $300 to $450 per day, but you must pay them for travel days. A common compromise is paying the full day rate for show days, and a half-rate ($150-$225) for pure travel days where they aren't mixing but are still driving or advancing.

For a 4-week US tour, it is almost always more cost-effective and logistically sound to carry your own production in a trailer rather than renting backline locally in every city. Renting a professional drum kit, bass rig, and two guitar amps locally can easily cost $400 to $600 per day. Over a 20-show run, that equates to $8,000 to $12,000 in rental fees, not including the daily headache of advancing the gear, hoping the local vendor provides the correct specs, and dialing in unfamiliar tones every night.

In contrast, renting a 5x8 or 6x10 enclosed cargo trailer from a company like U-Haul or a specialized tour outfitter for a month typically costs between $600 and $1,200 total. Even when you factor in the additional fuel costs (pulling a trailer reduces your van's fuel efficiency by about 3-5 MPG) and the cost of installing a hitch if you don't have one, the total expense of carrying a trailer will likely stay under $2,500 for the entire tour.

Beyond the financial savings, carrying your own gear provides immense peace of mind. Your band will perform better playing the instruments they know, your load-ins will be streamlined because your crew knows exactly how the trailer is packed, and your FOH engineer will have a consistent starting point for the mix every night. The only caveat is parking; you must advance trailer parking with every venue, as navigating a van and trailer in dense urban markets like NYC or Chicago requires careful planning.

I've never done a professional sound check before. What should I expect and how do I communicate with the sound engineer? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true,"artistProfile":{"goal":"fully-independent","stage":"emerging","genre":"singer-songwriter"}}]

A sound check is your chance to make the show sound great. Here's the protocol:

**The Sound Check Flow:**

1. **Line check (one instrument at a time):**
   - The engineer says 'give me kick' — play ONLY the kick drum steadily
   - They're setting gain, EQ, and gate/comp on each channel individually
   - When they say 'that's good,' move to the next instrument
   - Order: drums (kick, snare, toms, overheads), bass, guitars, keys, vocals

2. **Monitor check:**
   - After line check, the engineer dials in monitors
   - Tell them EXACTLY what you need: 'More vocal in my monitor, less guitar'
   - Use specific language: 'more,' 'less,' 'louder,' 'quieter' — not 'it sounds weird'
   - For singer-songwriters: you need YOUR vocal loud and clear in your monitor. Say: 'I need to hear myself clearly over everything else.'

3. **Play a song:**
   - Run through your LOUDEST song (the one with the most dynamic range)
   - This lets the engineer set the FOH (front of house) mix for your peak level
   - Play at PERFORMANCE volume — if you play quietly during sound check and loud during the show, the mix won't translate

**Communication Tips:**
- Be respectful and direct. 'Could I have more vocal in monitor 1, please?' > 'My monitor sucks.'
- The engineer is your ally. A good relationship = a better sounding show.
- If something sounds wrong during the set, make eye contact with the engineer and point to what needs adjusting. Don't stop playing to complain.
- Send your tech rider/input list IN ADVANCE. Engineers appreciate preparation.

**Singer-Songwriter Specific:**
- Bring your own DI box if you use an acoustic/electric
- Specify whether you want your vocal dry or with a touch of reverb in monitors
- If you use a capo, sound check with AND without it — tuning and tonal balance changes

We're in a 15-passenger van towing a 12-foot dual-axle trailer. How do I calculate our payload to ensure we aren't over the Gross Combined Weight Rating (GCWR)? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

Running `calculate_vehicle_payload` — vehicle: 15-passenger van, trailer: 12-foot dual-axle, metric: GCWR.

Calculating your Gross Combined Weight Rating (GCWR) is critical; exceeding it severely compromises your van's transmission, braking distance, and voids your liability insurance in the event of a crash. The GCWR is the maximum allowable combined weight of the tow vehicle, passengers, cargo, and the fully loaded trailer. You can find this number on the sticker inside the driver's side door jamb.

To calculate your actual weight, you must visit a commercial weigh station (like a CAT Scale at a truck stop) once fully loaded. First, weigh the entire rig to ensure you are under the GCWR. Next, weigh just the van's axles to ensure you aren't exceeding the van's Gross Vehicle Weight Rating (GVWR), which includes the band, merch, and the 'tongue weight' of the trailer pushing down on the hitch.

Proper weight distribution inside the trailer is vital. Approximately 60% of the cargo weight should be placed forward of the trailer's axles to maintain a tongue weight of 10-15% of the total trailer weight. If you load too much heavy backline behind the axles, the trailer will experience severe sway (fishtailing) at highway speeds, which is the leading cause of van-and-trailer accidents on tour.

- T-shirts: Your bread and butter. 2-3 designs.

We're bringing our US gear to Europe. Will our amps blow up? [Context: {"currentModule":"road"}]

US = 120V/60Hz. Europe = 220-240V/50Hz. Plugging US gear directly into European outlets WILL damage or destroy equipment.

Solution by gear type:
1. Pedals/Digital Gear: Most modern power supplies are 100-240V auto-switching. Check the label — if it says '100-240V' you just need a plug adapter, not a transformer.
2. Tube Amps: These are NOT auto-switching. You need a step-down transformer (220V to 120V). Must be rated for the amp's wattage PLUS 20% headroom. A 100W amp needs a 120W+ transformer. These are heavy (20-30 lbs).
3. Keyboards/Interfaces: Usually auto-switching. Verify on the power brick.
4. Drum machines/Rack gear: Check each unit individually.

Plug Adapter Types: UK = Type G (3 rectangular pins). EU = Type C/F (2 round pins). Switzerland = Type J.

Pro Tip: Rent a backline in Europe instead of bringing US amps overseas. The transformer weight and hassle often exceeds the rental cost.

What does 'walkout potential' mean on this promoter offer? It says Guarantee: $2,000, Walkout Potential: $4,500. [Context: {"currentModule":"touring","hasProject":true}]

[Mode A: Curriculum] 'Walkout potential' is the maximum amount of money you could theoretically leave the venue with if the show completely sells out. It is a combination of your upfront Guarantee plus your Backend (percentage of ticket sales after expenses).

Here is how the math works: The promoter subtracts the venue expenses (house nut), taxes, and their profit margin (promoter profit, usually 15%) from the gross ticket sales. This creates the 'Split Point'. Every dollar made *after* the split point is divided between you and the promoter—typically an 85/15 split in the artist's favor.

My booking agent says I need a proper technical rider for touring. I've never had one. What should it include and why does it matter? [Context: {"currentModule":"touring"}]

A rider is your contract with the venue for what they must provide. Without one, you arrive to whatever the venue decides to give you — which is often inadequate.

**The Two-Part Rider System:**

**Part 1: Technical Rider (the production requirements)**

**Stage plot:** A top-down diagram showing where each band member stands, equipment placement, and monitor positions. The sound engineer needs this before soundcheck.

**Input list:** Every microphone, DI box, and line input you need, numbered. Venues use this to set up their board.

Minimum content:
- PA system specifications (minimum wattage for your room sizes)
- Monitoring requirements (wedge monitors or in-ears, how many mixes)
- Microphone requirements (your specific needs — kick, snare, vocals, etc.)
- Backline requirements (if you need drums, bass amp, guitar amp provided)
- Stage dimensions required
- Advance information: soundcheck time request, load-in time

**Part 2: Hospitality Rider (the catering requirements)**
- Meals (usually 1–2 per show day)
- Drinks (water minimum — stay specific: 'still water, room temperature, 1 case')
- Dietary restrictions
- Towels, parking passes, guest list policy

**Why it matters:**
Venues with 50 shows per year know what's in a professional rider. Showing up without one signals 'emerging artist' and gets you the leftovers. A well-formatted rider signals professionalism and often gets you treated better than your fee would otherwise warrant.

**Calibrate to your deal size:** A $3K guarantee rider looks different from a festival rider. Start simple and build. Share your current setup and I'll draft a complete rider document.

How do I get booked for music festivals? I've applied to a bunch but never heard back. [Context: {"currentModule":"road","hasProject":true}]

Festival booking is competitive but very achievable for indie artists. Most artists fail because they target wrong and apply poorly. Here's the strategy:

Understand the tiers: Tier 1 (Coachella, Lollapalooza, Bonnaroo, ACL): You need an agent + significant streaming/draw numbers. Not realistic for most emerging indie artists. Tier 2 (SXSW, Treefort, Shaky Knees, Pitchfork Fest): Competitive but programmers actively seek emerging talent. This is your target zone. Tier 3 (Regional/local festivals, city fests, heritage fests): Most accessible. Often book through open applications. Great for building your festival resume. Start here.

Application timeline: Most festivals program 6-12 months in advance. Summer festivals (June-August) accept applications September-January. SXSW: deadline usually in September-October for March showcase. Apply EARLY — many festivals review on a rolling basis.

Your application must include: Professional EPK (electronic press kit): bio (2 paragraphs, not 10), high-res press photos (minimum 2), streaming links, social media links with follower counts, press quotes or notable placements, live video (THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT ELEMENT — festivals are booking a live experience). Streaming numbers and market-specific draw data. Any notable achievements (playlist placements, sync licenses, press features).

Where to apply: Sonicbids: Many festivals use this as their application portal. Annual membership ~$40. Direct applications: check festival websites for 'artist submissions' pages. Music Gorilla, GigSalad, ReverbNation opportunities: additional application portals. Showcases: SXSW, Folk Alliance, Americana Fest, CMJ — these are designed to connect artists with festival bookers.

Why you're not hearing back: (1) No live video or poor-quality video — this is the #1 rejection reason. (2) Applying to festivals way above your level. (3) Generic applications — customize every submission to explain why you fit THAT specific festival's audience. (4) Applying too late in the cycle. (5) No regional draw — festivals want artists who help sell tickets.

Pro tip: Attend the festival as a fan first. Meet bookers, stage managers, and other artists. Name-drop specific stages and past lineups in your application. 'I'd be a perfect fit for your [specific stage name] based on past bookings like [artist X and Y]' shows you've done your research.

How does show settlement work? I've been burned before by venues not paying what they promised. [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true,"artistProfile":{"goal":"fully-independent","stage":"developing","genre":"indie-rock"}}]

Show settlement is where independents most often lose money. Here's how to protect yourself:

**Settlement 101:**
Settlement happens after your set (or at the end of the night). You sit with the venue's business manager and reconcile the financials.

**What to Verify:**
1. **Ticket count:** How many tickets were sold? Request the actual ticket manifest or POS report — not a verbal number.
2. **Gross revenue:** Total door/ticket income BEFORE deductions.
3. **Deductions:** What's coming out? Sound engineer? Door person? Security? Promotion costs? These should have been agreed in advance.
4. **Your split:** After deductions, what's your share? Common splits:
   - Guarantee vs. door: you get either your guarantee OR your share of door, whichever is higher
   - Flat guarantee: fixed amount regardless of attendance
   - Percentage after expenses: 60/40, 70/30, 80/20 (headliner/opener)
5. **Merch:** Was there a merch cut? If so, subtract that from your merch income.

**The Settlement Sheet:**
Get EVERYTHING on paper (or documented digitally):
- Date, venue name, event name
- Ticket price(s), total tickets sold, comp tickets
- Gross revenue
- Itemized deductions
- Your payment amount
- Both parties sign

**Independent Artist Protection:**
- Take a PHOTO of the settlement sheet. Always.
- If the venue only does cash, count it IN FRONT of the venue manager.
- Never leave without settling. 'We'll mail you a check' is a red flag.
- If numbers seem wrong, ask to see the ticket manifest. You have the right.
- Keep a running settlement log across your tour — this becomes your tour P&L.

The hotel contract for our tour block says '20% allowable attrition'. What does that mean? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

Understanding the 'attrition rate' in your hotel block contract is critical to preventing massive, unexpected charges on your tour's master account.

When you negotiate a block of 20 rooms for your tour, the hotel takes those rooms off the public market. The 'allowable attrition' clause defines how many of those rooms you can cancel without a penalty. If the contract states '20% allowable attrition', it means you must 'pick up' (pay for) at least 80% of the block—in this case, 16 rooms.

If your crew decides to sleep on the bus and you only use 10 rooms, you will still be billed for the 6 unused rooms required to meet the 80% threshold. Your Tour Manager must actively manage the rooming list and release any unneeded rooms back to the hotel before the formal cutoff date (usually 30 days prior to arrival) to avoid these empty room penalties.

What does 'advancing a show' mean and how do I do it properly? My tour manager said I need to advance all my shows but I've never done it before. [Context: {"currentModule":"touring"}]

Advancing a show means confirming every logistical detail with the venue 7–14 days before the date — so there are no surprises on show day.

Most venues have a Production Manager or Stage Manager. Get their direct email/phone from the promoter. Do not advance through the promoter — they're the business layer; the production team is the operational layer.

**The Advance Checklist (confirm all of these):**

**Load-in/Logistics:**
- Load-in time (when can you enter and start setting up)
- Parking for the van/trailer — dedicated loading dock or street?
- Venue address, load-in door (often different from front entrance)
- Elevator/freight access for heavy gear

**Production:**
- Soundcheck time — confirmed, not approximate
- Stage plot accepted and understood
- Input list confirmed (do they have enough channels? Do they have specific mics you need?)
- Backline confirmation (if venue is providing)
- In-ear monitor mix availability or wedge monitors?

**Hospitality:**
- Meals — what's provided and at what time
- Dressing room access — private vs. shared?
- Guest list — how many, what's the process night-of
- Merch setup — where, split percentage confirmed

**Show logistics:**
- Doors time / set times
- Curfew (hard curfew vs. soft)
- Who to check in with on arrival
- Night-of contact phone number

**Format:** Send the advance via email with your stage plot, input list, and rider attached. Request confirmation in writing. Keep the response — if they confirm something and then don't provide it, you have documentation.

I keep having problems on tour — missed show times, accounting errors at settlement, crew conflicts. My manager says I need a tour manager. Is this worth it at my level and what should I look for? [Context: {"currentModule":"touring"}]

The problems you're describing — missed show times, settlement errors, crew conflicts — are exactly what tour managers solve. The question is whether the ROI justifies the cost at your current tour income level.

**What a Tour Manager Does:**
- Advances all shows (confirms every logistical detail with venues in advance)
- Night-of settlement (they handle the financial reconciliation with the promoter — no more errors)
- Daily logistics (hotel check-ins, load-in times, routing decisions)
- Band/crew management (the interpersonal layer you shouldn't be managing from stage)
- Accounting (daily expense tracking, cash management, per diems)
- Emergency triage (when things go wrong, they handle it so you can focus on performing)

**When it's worth it:**
Rule of thumb: If your average daily tour income (guarantee + merch) is more than $500/day, a tour manager is worth having. Their daily rate ($200–400/day for emerging act TMs) is recovered by the efficiency gains and errors they prevent.

Missed show times and settlement errors are the most expensive problems a TM solves — a single underpaid settlement or a missed show can cost more than a TM's entire tour fee.

**What to look for:**
- Experience with your tour size (don't hire someone who's only worked major arena tours for a 400-cap club run — different skill sets)
- References from artists at your level
- Strong organizational systems (ask to see their advance template)
- Emergency problem-solving stories during the interview — how they handled a crisis tells you more than their resume

**Rate:** $200–350/day all-in for an emerging act TM, plus hotel room, per diem, and travel.

At what point does it make financial sense to upgrade from a Sprinter van with hotels to a sleeper tour bus? [Context: {"currentModule":"agent","hasProject":true}]

[Mode A: Curriculum] The jump from a Sprinter van to a sleeper bus is the biggest financial leap an artist makes on the road. The tipping point is rarely about comfort—it’s a pure numbers game based on your daily touring overhead versus your nightly guarantees.

A Sprinter van costs roughly $250/day. Add 4 hotel rooms at $150/each ($600), plus fuel, and your daily transport/lodging overhead is about $900-$1,000. 

A standard 12-bunk sleeper bus starts around $1,200-$1,500/day. However, you must also pay the driver's day rate ($250-$350), their hotel room on days off, bus fuel (which is double the cost of a van), generator fuel, and daily parking/shore power fees. Your daily overhead on a bus easily hits $2,000-$2,500.

Financial sense kicks in when your touring party exceeds 8 people (making hotel blocks astronomically expensive), your routing requires overnight 500+ mile drives that a single van driver cannot legally or safely do, and your nightly show guarantees consistently exceed $5,000. Until then, the Sprinter remains your most profitable vehicle.

The show just ended. The promoter handed me a settlement sheet showing $4,200 in expenses — way higher than the $1,500 they originally quoted. They're saying I owe money back. What do I do? [Context: {"currentModule":"touring"}]

Do NOT sign the settlement sheet until you've reviewed and challenged it.

**Immediate steps:**

**1. Request itemized receipts for every expense line.** 'Sound' for $800 is not an acceptable expense entry — you need: sound engineer receipt, backline rental receipt, stage manager invoice. They must be able to produce actual receipts, not estimates.

**2. Challenge against your contract.** Does your contract specify an expense cap? If it does and they've exceeded it, the overage is the promoter's liability — not yours. The $1,500 they quoted should be in writing.

**3. If no cap was written:** This is a lesson in why expense caps must be in contracts. However, you can still challenge obviously inflated items:
- Marketing expenses: Did you agree in advance to marketing spend on your behalf?
- Production upgrades: Did you request production beyond the rider? If not, unapproved production upgrades are the promoter's cost.
- Venue staff overtime: Was your show schedule maintained? If the show ran long due to venue operations, overtime is their cost.

**4. Your walk-away position:** Calculate the minimum you leave with:
- If your guarantee was $3,000 and you're on percentage against expenses — your guarantee is your floor. The promoter owes you at least $3,000 regardless of their expense claims if they didn't cap expenses in the contract.

**5. Escalation:** If they refuse to honor the guarantee, tell them you will not return to this market and will report the settlement dispute to your booking agent. Promoter reputation matters — this is leverage.

Do not accept cash with an unfair settlement sheet. Hold the settlement open and revisit in the morning with documentation.

Venue closure 2 weeks out is a serious breach of your booking contract. Here's how to respond.

**2. Ticket refunds:** Your ticketing platform (Eventbrite, Ticketmaster, etc.) has specific protocols for venue closures. Contact them immediately — they typically issue automatic refunds to buyers and release you from liability IF the cancellation is venue-initiated.

**3. Communicate with ticket holders within 24 hours.** Your audience needs to hear from you before discovering the cancellation from a third party. The message: 'Due to an unexpected venue closure, [show] has been cancelled. Refunds will be issued automatically. We're working to rebook — stay tuned.' This protects your reputation regardless of the business dispute.

**Short-term options:**
**Rebook at a nearby alternative venue.** 2 weeks is tight but possible for a comparable room in the same market. Contact your booking agent today — they have relationships with competing venues. Ticket holders who haven't yet refunded may transfer.

**Postpone with a future date.** 'Cancelled' has worse optics than 'postponed to [date]' even when you don't have the date confirmed yet.

**Financial recovery:**
- Your tour insurance (if you have it) may cover direct costs (routing, accommodation deposits)
- Your contract with the venue — did it include a force majeure clause, or was the closure due to their business failure? Business failure is typically NOT force majeure and creates venue liability for your costs.

Document all expenses incurred for this show before any settlement conversation.

If you reach the end of the tour without touching the contingency fund, that money rolls directly into the tour's net profit. Never use contingency funds to buy nicer dinners or upgrade a hotel room; its sole purpose is to ensure the tour doesn't collapse if disaster strikes.

UK is not Schengen. US citizens can visit the UK visa-free for 6 months but 'performing for pay' requires a Certificate of Sponsorship from a UK employer/promoter AND a Creative Worker visa application filed in advance. This typically takes 3–8 weeks to process and costs £244 application fee. If your UK promoter is established, they should know how to sponsor your work authorization — insist on this before booking UK shows.

**Practical border reality:**
The German and French customs occasionally question touring musicians about work status. Having the promoter letters and itinerary makes the conversation short. 'Performing at X venue on [date]' backed by paperwork is almost always waved through.

I'm doing just 4 shows in Germany. My gear is worth $12,000. My touring agent says to skip the ATA Carnet because it's 'too much hassle' for one country and to just use a 'Temporary Import Permit' instead. Is that right?
